claims.text: The starting alloy is chemically homogeneous.
The as-cast starting alloy has a high degree of atomic-scale disorder.
Controlled annealing and quenching can induce partial atomic ordering in the alloy.
The proposed thermal treatments can alter ordering without changing the overall composition.
Post-synthesis thermal treatment modifies the degree of local atomic order or clustering.
Reducing atomic-scale disorder reduces electron scattering and localization effects.
Increasing short-range atomic order enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling facilitates more effective Cooper pairing.
More effective Cooper pairing raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Reducing atomic-scale disorder sharpens the superconducting transition.
Optimal annealing that produces moderate short-range order will cause a modest but measurable increase in Tc relative to the as-cast state.
Annealing-induced ordering may change the upper critical field.
Tc will increase systematically as structural signatures of ordering become evident.
Narrower XRD peak widths are an indicator of increased short-range atomic ordering.
The as-cast baseline has an established Tc measured by resistivity and magnetic susceptibility.
The expected Tc shift is approximately a fraction of a kelvin to about 1 K.
The hypothesis is limited to treatments that produce partial ordering without phase segregation, precipitation, or major compositional inhomogeneity.
Failure to observe an ordering-correlated increase in Tc, or observation of a reversed trend, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The query requests an alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, whereas the baseline states that the selected as-cast alloy already has an established Tc from resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.

The predicted outcome invokes an optimum at moderate ordering, which can imply a non-monotonic response across a broad ordering series, while the falsification rule declares any non-monotonic trend falsifying.
